text:
Short answer: on its own, no. It's context, not evidence — and if you lead with it, you'll weaken a case that may have better foundations elsewhere.

**Why the panel composition proves little**

Senior risk and finance roles at banks are still heavily male at the level people get picked for interview panels. An all-male panel of four is roughly what you'd expect by chance from that population — it doesn't require any discriminatory intent or process to produce. A tribunal, ombudsman, or a sympathetic HR director will all know this. Panel composition can corroborate a pattern once you've shown something substantive, but it can't do the work by itself, and arguing from it alone tends to read as "I lost, therefore bias," which gets you dismissed quickly.

It is, though, a legitimate thing to raise as a process observation — many banks have their own internal policy requiring mixed panels for senior appointments. If they breached their own policy, that's a procedural failure you can point at without alleging anything about motive. Worth checking what their published recruitment or diversity policy actually says.

**The credential gap is also weaker than it looks**

I'd push back gently here. "Head of risk modelling" at a bank is often not primarily a modelling job. It's model governance, model risk frameworks, defending methodology to supervisors, validation cycles, committee politics, and owning the relationship with the regulator through approval and remediation processes. A master's in finance plus deep regulatory-affairs experience can genuinely be the better fit for that, and a PhD in statistics plus nine years building models can read to a panel as technically excellent but untested on the parts of the role that actually consume the time.

That may well be wrong in your case — you may have been doing exactly that regulatory work for years. But you should assume that's the story they'll tell, and work out now whether you can rebut it with specifics or whether it's broadly fair. Also, don't over-read the announcement wording: that's internal comms copy, written to flatter the appointee, not a record of the panel's reasoning.

**The silence is the more interesting fact**

Two weeks with no response to a written request for reasons is the thing I'd actually pursue. It may be nothing — HR teams go quiet on these out of caution and slowness far more often than out of guilt. But unexplained refusal to give reasons is the kind of thing that lets an inference be drawn later, and chasing it is low-cost and entirely reasonable regardless.

I'd send a short, unemotional follow-up that:

- References your original request and its date
- Asks for the selection criteria used, the weighting, and your scores against each
- Asks who to escalate to if feedback isn't forthcoming
- Says nothing about the panel's gender and makes no allegation

Keep it the kind of email you'd be comfortable having read aloud. If they answer, you'll learn whether the criteria they cite match the ones in the job advert. Criteria that shifted between the posting and the decision — particularly if they shifted toward the successful candidate's profile — is a far stronger signal than anything about the panel.

**One practical question for you**

What do you want out of this? Feedback that makes you a better candidate next time, an internal path to a similar role, or redress? Those pull in different directions, and the discrimination framing is costly if you're staying in the organisation or the industry. It's sometimes worth the cost. It's rarely worth paying before you've seen the reasons.

Were you an internal candidate, and which jurisdiction is this? Both change what's available to you and how long you have to act — time limits for formal complaints can be short.
